chapter: Pranks, the Mingus fight and Duke's writing
title: Which sidemen really wrote Duke's music
summary: Tizol says men like Rex Stewart, Hodges, Carney and Cootie mostly shaped phrasing rather than wrote, and credits Jimmy Hamilton and Strayhorn.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: In this section about the 1930's, Mercer says, 'When you look at the credits of his compositions (he means Duke's compositions from this period) you will see several of the side men credited as collaborators. None was probably so creative or prolific as Bubber Miley, but men like Johnnie Hodges, Barney Bigard, Harry Carney, Juan Tizol, Rex Stewart and Cootie Williams had ideas -- contributed them, often to head arrangements, and were credited.' Is that right?
That's right.
Did Bubber Miley do a lot of writing?
I don't know; I was not there when Bubber Miley was in the band.
And ...
They didn't get credit all the time for what they did, did they, Juan? Duke didn't give everybody credit for what they did in the writing; you know he didn't.
But I mean, the boys didn't write anything, but they used to play -- they used to do his composition in the way they were playing of phrasing it or something like that.
Well, they got your name in there, and you didn't get any credit for anything. Your own compositions.
Well, somebody must have given me credit, I don't know.
Rex did some writing; I mean, Rex actually did write.
Rex did some writing.
Didn't he? Didn't Rex write music?
I'm sorry to say, but I don't know anything about Rex ever doing any writing.
Well, I've seen his composer credits, but maybe that was from head arrangements; from things that he played?
Because Rex, I used to fuss many times with him, because I used to do all the copying and all the extractions, I knew what Rex was supposed to be playing, and

Rex was a man -- he got a terrific -- for doing things, you know, to play anything he wants to, and he could ad lib a lot of things, and he could play anything. But nobody ever paid attention -- but I was paying attention, and I said the only note that is not doubled in the brass section is you, and you are not playing those notes there, you know?
I see. He played what he wanted to play, then?

Yeah, he played what he wanted to play, because he could do it; he had that ability -- to go over there and play on the trumpet and go with the brass section and say, 'If you don't pay any attention, fine, that's all right'.
And I know that Barney did some writing.
Yeah ...
Did Johnny Rider just write or improvise?

Johnny used to play on the saxophone, and I used to take it down for him and write it, like even on the show, I used to pass him a piece of music; I used to write things for him. The melody, but nothing else. I used to write the melody for him, you know?
Oh, I see. And Harry Carney -- he didn't do much writing, did he?
I don't know if Harry did -- I don't think so. I don't think so, maybe he did some and I didn't
know about them.
Well, I only know of a couple of things. And Cootie?
Cootie, also; I don't believe he wrote anything.

I just thought it was kind of funny that all of these people were grouped with you when you were actually writing. That's what I wanted to ask you about, because I thought that maybe they were doing more than I knew about -- the other people he named didn't do much writing.
No, I don't think. The only one, while I was in the band, is the clarinet player, what was his name?
Jimmie Hamilton?
Oh, Jimmy Hamilton. He wrote himself, some stuff and I arranged some things for the band.
I'm trying to remember -- what did Jimmie write? Do you remember?

No, I don't know. I don't know what he wrote, but I know he used to write for the brass or the saxaphones, and so forth like that; it was very nice. But I don't know if it was his own composition or what.
And then really, the other major writer was Billy Strayhorn when he arrived.
Oh, yeah. He was Duke Ellington's right hand man.
